chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from Ali ibn Isma'il from Muhammad ibn Umar from Ali ibn al-Husayn from Hariz from Abu Ubaydah who said:

I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man gave a man one thousand dirhams to mix with his own wealth and trade with it. He said: When he asked for it from him, he said: The wealth is gone, and he had with him something similar belonging to someone else, and much wealth belonging to another. I said: What did those do? He said: They took their wealth. Abu Ja'far and Abu Abdillah (peace be upon them both) said together: 'He returns to him with his wealth, and he returns to those with what they took.'
7 - Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Kufi from Muhammad ibn Isma'il from Ja'far ibn Isa who said:

I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), 'May I be your ransom,' regarding a woman who dies and her father claims that he had loaned her some of the belongings and servants she had. Is his claim accepted without evidence, or is his claim not accepted except with evidence? He wrote to him (peace be upon him): 'It is valid without evidence.' He said: And I wrote to him: If the husband of the deceased woman, and her father-in-law, and her mother-in-law, claim regarding her belongings or servants that they are similar to what her father claimed regarding the loan of some of the belongings or servants, are they in the same position as the father in the claim? He wrote: 'No.'

key_terms.يَخْلِطُهَا بِمَالِهِ: mixing it with his wealth (commingling funds)

ai.seo_question: What is the legal ruling on mixed trade funds and claims of loaned items from a deceased woman's estate?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the practical application of evidentiary standards in Shia jurisprudence, highlighting the principle of *al-bayyinah 'ala al-mudda'i* (the burden of proof is on the claimant) with specific exceptions. The first ruling emphasizes the protection of capital in mixed trade partnerships, ensuring that loss does not equate to forfeiture when equivalent assets are present. The second ruling distinguishes between the privileged status of a father claiming borrowed items from his deceased daughter versus other relatives, reflecting the nuanced hierarchy of kinship in inheritance and property disputes.
